clinicalPearls: Presents with multiple discrete, hard keratotic papules scattered across the palms and soles, sometimes with central depressions when the plug is removed
The classic type 1 (Buschke-Fischer-Brauer) is autosomal dominant and caused by variants in AAGAB
Lesions tend to be more numerous and prominent over pressure points and can be tender when walking
Onset is usually in adolescence or early adulthood, and lesions accumulate slowly over time
Some case series report an association with internal malignancy, so age-appropriate cancer awareness is reasonable, though the link is debated
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by family history, dermoscopy and biopsy showing a compact column of hyperkeratosis; AAGAB testing can confirm type 1
Management is supportive with keratolytics, paring, emollients and, in resistant cases, oral retinoids
reference.pathophysiology: Punctate palmoplantar keratoderma type 1 is caused by loss-of-function variants in AAGAB, which encodes alpha- and gamma-adaptin binding protein p34, a regulator of intracellular vesicle trafficking and of the recycling of growth factor receptors such as the epidermal growth factor receptor. Haploinsufficiency is thought to enhance keratinocyte proliferation in focal areas of acral skin, producing discrete columns of compact hyperkeratosis that clinically appear as punctate keratotic papules concentrated at sites of pressure.
additionalDifferentials: Cole disease and other punctate keratoderma variants
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of AAGAB for type 1 disease
Skin biopsy showing a compact column of orthohyperkeratosis overlying a depressed epidermis
Dermoscopy to distinguish keratotic plugs from warts
Age-appropriate malignancy screening awareness given reported associations
Clinical photography to monitor lesion accumulation
redFlags: New systemic symptoms or signs prompting age-appropriate malignancy evaluation given reported associations
Rapidly changing or ulcerating individual lesions
Secondary infection of pared or fissured lesions
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and chronic; lesions persist and slowly increase in number, but with keratolytic and mechanical treatment most patients maintain good function.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating the papules as recalcitrant plantar warts
Overlooking the family history that points to a dominant keratoderma
Dismissing the debated malignancy association without age-appropriate review
Escalating to systemic retinoids before adequate topical keratolytic therapy
management: Reduce hyperkeratosis with topical keratolytics such as salicylic acid or urea preparations and regular emollients
Offer mechanical paring or debridement of keratotic plugs and pressure-offloading footwear or padding to relieve tenderness on walking
Consider systemic retinoids such as acitretin for extensive or refractory disease
Provide genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal dominant AAGAB-related condition
Maintain age-appropriate malignancy awareness given the reported, though debated, association with internal cancers
Monitor lesion accumulation clinically, using dermoscopy to distinguish plugs from viral warts
